OREGON STATE GAME COMMISSION
comments on
ENDANGERED SPECIES CONSERVATION ACT OF 1972
The Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1972 states as its objective:
"To provide for the conservation, protection, and propagation of species or subspecies of fish and wildlife that are threatened with extinction or likely within the foreseeable future to become threatened with extinction."
Provisions of the Act instruct the Secretary to acquire land; cooperate with the States; control import, export or interstate shipment; and enforce regulations pertaining to endangered species or those threatened with extinction. To accomplish these measures, the Act authorizes the Secretary to assume management responsibility for all wildlife species appearing on the endangered or threatened lists. The Secretary presently has jurisdiction for migratory birds and mammals and the States have management responsibility for resident species. State jurisdiction was recognized by remarks on predator control given by Assistant Secretary Nathaniel Reed at the North American Wildlife and Natural Resources Conference in Mexico. The transfer of this authority to the federal government is not consistent with Mr. Reed's statements.
The Secretary already has the authority, through Public Law 89-669, to acquire lands for the conservation, protection and propagation of species threatened with extinction. The Endangered Species Conservation Act merely deletes current ceilings on the acquisition of habitat. Public Law 89-669 further instructs the Secretary to cooperate with the States through consultation prior to acquiring lands and by entering into agreements for administering and managing such areas.
Public Law 91-135 authorizes the Secretary to control import and export of endangered species and to prevent interstate shipment of species taken contrary to State law. The Endangered Species Conservation Act would expand the Secretary's authority to regulate importation of species taken on the high seas, an authority he does not now possess.
Passage of amendments to delete current ceilings in P. L. 89-669 and to give the Secretary authority to regulate importation of animals taken on the high seas in P. L. 91-135 could more readily be obtained than could passage of new legislation. These amendments would then give the Secretary all authority contained in the Endangered Species Conservation for all endangered or threatened species.
